opus-5.5.text:
I think what's really interesting is that formal theorem proving is, in a sense, the cleanest possible version of the problem coding agents are trying to solve. When you write a proof in Lean, you're writing code, and the proof checker gives you a perfect, binary signal: either the proof compiles and it's correct, or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity, no "it looks right to me." That's something you almost never get in general software engineering, where you have tests that are incomplete, specifications that are fuzzy, and a lot of judgment about what "correct" even means.

So for a long time, theorem proving was a really nice sandbox for studying reasoning and search. Back when we were working on things like HyperTree Proof Search, the core idea was that you could have a model propose proof steps, verify them with the formal system, and use that feedback to do search and to improve the model over time. And that loop—generate, verify, learn from the verifier—is essentially the same loop you want for coding agents. The agent writes some code, runs it, looks at compiler errors or test failures, and iterates.

What I find fascinating is how much the two directions transfer. On one side, the techniques you develop for theorem proving—search over long chains of steps, using a verifier as a reward signal, dealing with very sparse success—are exactly what you need when an agent has to fix a bug across a large codebase over many steps. On the other side, as models got much better at code in general, they also got much better at formal math, because Lean is just a programming language with a very strict type checker. A lot of the progress in formal theorem proving recently came from simply having stronger code models underneath.

And I think there's a deeper point, too. One of the big bottlenecks for coding agents is verification: how do you know the agent actually did the right thing? In math, the formal system solves that for you. In software, we don't have that yet for most code. So one direction I find exciting is whether you can bring more of that formal flavor into coding—stronger specifications, better tests generated automatically, maybe even partial formal verification—so that agents get a reward signal that's closer to what you have in Lean. If you get that, you can train much more effectively with reinforcement learning, because the model can't just fool itself into thinking it succeeded.

So for me, theorem proving was never really just about math. It was about building systems that can reason over long horizons and check their own work, and coding agents are the place where that matters most in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for me these two things are really the same problem viewed from two angles. When I was at Meta working on HyperTree Proof Search and formal math, the thing that made it work was that Lean or Isabelle gives you a perfect verifier. You propose a tactic, the environment tells you immediately whether it's valid, and when you close the goal you know with certainty the proof is correct. There is no ambiguity, no human in the loop to judge. And that is exactly what you want for reinforcement learning, because you have an infinite source of clean reward.

Coding is interesting because it's almost that, but not quite. You have compilers, you have type checkers, you have unit tests, so you get a signal that's much richer than what you get in natural language. But the signal is noisy. Tests can pass while the code is wrong, tests can be incomplete, and the specification itself is often fuzzy. So a lot of what we learned in theorem proving transfers directly: how to do search over long trajectories, how to handle sparse rewards where you only know at the end whether you succeeded, how to generate your own training data by having the model attempt problems and keeping what verifies. Those recipes are the same.

The other direction is maybe more interesting to me now. Formal proving taught us that when the model knows it will be checked, it behaves very differently. It stops hallucinating, because hallucinating doesn't get rewarded. With coding agents, the trend is to give the model more and more of that verification structure, let it run the code, see the error, iterate. And I think the end state is that writing software will look more and more like writing a proof. You state what you want precisely, the agent searches for something that satisfies it, and a verifier closes the loop. The gap right now is that we don't have the Lean of software engineering, the specification language is still English, and that's the part I find both frustrating and exciting.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that theorem proving gives you a very clear feedback loop. You propose a proof, and the proof checker tells you whether it is valid. If it fails, you get information that can help you revise it. That’s very close to what a coding agent does when it writes a program, runs it, looks at the errors, and tries again.

But in software, passing the tests doesn’t necessarily mean you solved the problem. The tests may be incomplete. In formal mathematics, if the proof checks, you know that it establishes the statement you formalized. Of course, you still have to make sure that statement captures what you intended.

So theorem proving is a really interesting environment for developing agents that can reason over many steps, use tools, and recover from mistakes. And the connection goes both ways: better coding agents can help build formal proofs, while techniques developed for theorem proving could help coding agents produce software with stronger correctness guarantees.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting connection is that, in both cases, you’re generating something that you can execute and get feedback on. For a coding agent, you can run the code, run tests, look at errors, and iterate. In formal theorem proving, you propose a proof and the proof assistant tells you whether it’s valid, or what remains to be proved.

The big difference is the strength of that feedback. Your code can pass all the tests and still be wrong. With a formal proof, once the kernel accepts it, you have a much stronger guarantee that you’ve established the statement you wrote down. Of course, you still need to make sure that statement captures what you actually wanted.

So theorem proving gives you a very interesting environment for studying agents: how they explore, break a problem into intermediate steps, and recover when an approach fails. And those are also central challenges in coding. It’s not just about producing the next few lines; it’s about making progress toward a goal over many steps, using feedback along the way.
